performed_via_github_app.description:
Codecov provides highly integrated tools to group, merge, archive and compare coverage reports. Whether your team is comparing changes in a pull request or reviewing a single commit, Codecov will improve the code review workflow and quality.

## Code coverage done right.®

1. Upload coverage reports from your CI builds.
2. Codecov merges all builds and languages into one beautiful coherent report.
3. Get commit statuses, pull request comments and coverage overlay via our browser extension.

When Codecov merges your uploads it keeps track of the CI provider (inc. build details) and user specified context, e.g. `#unittest` ~ `#smoketest` or `#oldcode` ~ `#newcode`. You can track the `#unittest` coverage independently of other groups. [Learn more here](
http://docs.codecov.io/docs/flags)

Through **Codecov's Browser Extension** reports overlay directly in GitHub UI to assist in code review in [Chrome](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/detail/codecov/gedikamndpbemklijjkncpnolildpbgo) or Firefox (https://addons.mozilla.org/en-US/firefox/addon/codecov/)

*Highly detailed* **pull request comments** and *customizable* **commit statuses** will improve your team's workflow and code coverage incrementally.

**File backed configuration** all through the `codecov.yml`. 

## FAQ
- Do you **merge multiple uploads** to the same commit? **Yes**
- Do you **support multiple languages** in the same project? **Yes**
- Can you **group coverage reports** by project and/or test type? **Yes**
- How does **pricing** work? Only paid users can view reports and post statuses/comments.

body:
## Result: blocked on missing C stubs, not on the evaluator

The Wasm module **builds and loads**, then fails at link with **53 unimplemented primitives**:

| group | count | what it is |
|---|---|---|
| `ml_z_*` | 27 | zarith (arbitrary-precision integers) |
| `Base_*` | 19 | Jane Street Base: hashing, int-math intrinsics |
| `bin_prot_*` | 2 | Bin_prot blit stubs |
| `expect_test_collector_*` | 2 | Jane Street test collector |
| other | 3 | `caml_csel_value`, `caml_out_channel_pos_fd`, `time_now_*` |

Root cause: Hazel's `Int` and `Nat` are arbitrary-precision — `language` reaches `Bigint` from six files, including `BuiltinsBase.re` where the integer builtins are defined — so `bignum` is load-bearing for the *semantics*, not an incidental dependency that could be dropped to get a benchmark number. And `bignum` drags in zarith *plus* the whole Jane Street `Core`/`Base` C-stub surface. Under `js_of_ocaml` all of it is satisfied by hand-written JS runtimes (`zarith_stubs_js`, which this repo further patches — see `make setup-zarith`). Those do not port to `wasm_of_ocaml`.

Passing the existing JS runtimes to the wasm build via `(wasm_of_ocaml (javascript_files ...))` made essentially no difference (54 → 53). Dune accepts the field; whether the files are honoured at all is unconfirmed. The copy rules are left in because they're the right shape for a fix, not because they worked.

**No performance number was obtained, and none is obtainable without clearing this first.**

### Ways forward

1. Wasm-compatible runtimes for all 53 — most plausibly porting the existing JS stubs to wasm_of_ocaml's calling convention.
2. Build real zarith/GMP for Wasm — addresses the 27 `ml_z_*`, but not the 26 Jane Street ones.
3. **Drop `bignum` from the evaluator's cone**: a `Bigint` backend over JS `BigInt`. This removes zarith *and* Core in one move, and is the only option that also helps an Internet Computer port, where the problem is strictly worse — no JS host to fall back on at all.

Option 3 looks the most tractable, and is worth considering on its own merits regardless of Wasm.

### What is nonetheless usable here

- **The `util` split is real and green.** `language`'s dependency closure is now `util → {ptmap, bignum, uuidm, unionFind, csv}` — no Bonsai, no `virtual_dom`. Web-side directories uniformly `open Util_web` (which re-exports `Util`), so moving a module between the two libraries no longer causes call-site churn.
- **js_of_ocaml 5→6 portability debt is now mapped.** The two versions disagree in ways that bite: `Firebug` exists only in 5.x and `Console` only in 6.x; `setTimeout` changed from `(Js.callback, Js.number_t)` to `(Js.meth_callback, float)`; `scrollTop`/`Date`/`performance` return `Js.number_t` where they returned `float`/`int`. Surviving uses go through `Js.Unsafe` so one source compiles under both. This is what a future jsoo upgrade will cost.
- **`uuidm 0.9.8` transitively caps how new a js_of_ocaml Hazel can use** (via `topkg → cmdliner < 2.0`), which is why the switch pins 6.2.0 rather than 6.4.1.
- **A reproducible Bonsai-free switch recipe**, in `bench/wasm/setup-switch.sh`. Getting it to solve required the `archive` opam repo, pinning every shared package to what the main switch resolved to, and dropping `bisect_ppx`.

### Verification

| check | result |
|---|---|
| `dune build src bench --profile release` (ordinary switch) | clean |
| `@test-quick` | 3457 tests, 0 failures |
| `language` closure Bonsai-free | yes |
| Wasm module builds and loads | yes |
| Wasm module links | **no** — 53 missing primitives |

Still **not for merge**: the livelit deletion is a deliberate shortcut, and the principled version registers livelit views from the web layer instead.

## Update: ~4× faster, on fixed-precision workloads

Following the earlier bignum wall — the way through was to lean on Hazel's *fixed-precision* types. `Int`/`Nat` are `Bigint`-backed, but `SInt` (machine int) and `Float` are not, so workloads written in those avoid zarith entirely.

Both backends built from **js_of_ocaml 6.2.0**, node 22, 20 iterations. **Result checksums match across backends**, so this measures the same computation and not a silently-stuck one.

| workload | js_of_ocaml | wasm_of_ocaml | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|
| `sint-fib` (recursion) | 1050 ms | 285 ms | **3.7×** |
| `sint-fib` incr | 1053 ms | 276 ms | **3.8×** |
| `float-numeric` (alloc-light) | 290 ms | 74 ms | **3.9×** |
| `float-numeric` incr | 303 ms | 71 ms | **4.3×** |
| `sint-list` (alloc-heavy) | 168 ms | 42 ms | **4.0×** |
| `sint-list` incr | 162 ms | 41 ms | **3.9×** |

The differences *between* workloads are **not** resolvable from this data — across two runs the ordering flipped (`sint-list` lowest in one, highest in the other). The ~4× headline is solid; please don't read a profile effect into the breakdown.

### What getting bignum out of the way exposed

- `Statics.re` had **exactly one** use of Jane Street Core (`Core.Memo.general`). Replacing it with a local `Util.Memo` removed Core from the evaluator's cone entirely.
- `Sets`, `AST`, `Parser.mly` and `Lexer.mll` reached the `bignum` package directly; they now go through `util`'s `BigInt` wrapper, which is portable across both builds.
- The stub keeps construction/comparison total (`Builtins.ctx_init` needs them to boot) and makes **arithmetic raise**, so a workload reaching `Int`/`Nat` fails loudly rather than quietly benchmarking 63-bit math.

### Relationship to #1131

#1131 (*Port to wasm_of_ocaml*, open since Nov 2023) hit the same wall we did: Bonsai pins an older `js_of_ocaml`, and `wasm_of_ocaml` needs a newer one. That thread pursues **moving Bonsai forward** — newer Bonsai is OxCaml-first, ReasonML doesn't work with OxCaml, then bleeding-edge Bonsai with `basement` C-stub failures on Mac.

This PR takes the other route: **cut the evaluator out of the Bonsai cone and port only the compute core.** Bonsai never has to move. That's what the `util`/`util_web` split and the livelit removal buy.

Three findings from here that may be useful over there:

1. **Bonsai is not the last blocker, and zarith is worse.** Behind Bonsai sit 27 `ml_z_*` primitives plus the Core C-stub surface. A whole-app port solves Bonsai and then hits this immediately; an evaluator-only port only has to solve this one.
2. **`uuidm 0.9.8 → topkg → cmdliner < 2.0` caps `js_of_ocaml` at 6.2.x**, independently of Bonsai.
3. **Fixed-precision Hazel already runs in Wasm, at ~4×.** That number exists today without resolving either blocker.

### Arbitrary precision: the remaining work

Full-fidelity Hazel in Wasm still needs a bignum. The most promising route is the one Motoko took — a bignum compiled to Wasm, linked against the compiler output. The wrinkle is that `wasm_of_ocaml` represents OCaml values as **Wasm GC** structs while a C bignum lives in **linear memory**; unlike Motoko, which controlled both sides, this needs a copy-in/copy-out shim at the boundary. `wasm_of_ocaml`'s `.wat` runtime hook looks like the seam to try.

### Correction to an earlier note

I previously suggested the evaluator lacked TCO. That was wrong. [`Trampoline.re`](../blob/wasm-eval-bench-spike/src/language/dynamics/evaluation/Trampoline.re) is an explicit stack machine — object-language call depth lives in a heap-allocated callstack — and measured under js_of_ocaml, both tail *and* non-tail Hazel recursion reach depth 20000+. Deep recursion is not a backend risk. The stack overflow that prompted the claim was a mis-typed workload (an `SInt` counter inside `use Float in`), not a depth limit.

### Verification

`dune build src bench --profile release` clean on the ordinary switch; `@test-quick` 3457 tests passing. Still **not for merge** — the livelit deletion remains a deliberate shortcut.

## Revised: settings axis added, and a caveat on what the number means

A fair challenge was raised on the numbers above: benchmarking headless Hazel may mislead, because a lot of what makes Hazel slow is the extra per-expression information statics and evaluation record for the UI. That's right, and it prompted two changes plus a sharper claim.

Two questions were tangled together, and they have different answers.

### Is the comparison between backends fair? Yes.

This is what the harness is built to guarantee: **one source tree, one settings record, one opam switch, one compiler version** — the only thing that differs is the backend flag. The result checksums confirm both sides computed the same answer. A lean path doesn't threaten this; it just has to be the *same* lean path on both sides, and it is.

### Does ~3.5× predict how much faster the app would feel? No.

This measures the evaluator alone — no zipper, no vdom, no editor. End-to-end speedup would be diluted by whatever share of real time is spent outside this path. Rather than assume that away, two probes were added:

**A settings axis.** `probe_all` governs how much per-expression information statics and evaluation record for the UI. It is **off even in `CoreSettings.on`**, so the earlier numbers measured a leaner path than the editor actually runs. Both profiles are now reported — and they are **indistinguishable on these workloads**. So the probe machinery is not what's slow here. That doesn't refute the concern; it narrows where the cost can be hiding.

**A cold statics sample.** `Statics.mk` is memoized (via `Util.Memo`), so it can only be timed cold — a loop measures cache hits, which is what a first attempt did, producing meaningless 6–12× "speedups" on ~0.0 ms. The harness now emits `statics-cold-1shot`, but it is a single unrepeated sample visibly dominated by JIT warm-up: the *same program* measured 16.6 ms under one profile and 3.2 ms under another. **No conclusions should be drawn from it.** Qualitatively it supports only that statics is single-digit ms here while evaluation is hundreds.

### Updated results

Both backends from js_of_ocaml 6.2.0, node 22, 20 iterations, checksums matching.

| workload | profile | js_of_ocaml | wasm_of_ocaml | speedup |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sint-fib` plain | probes-off | 1020 ms | 341 ms | 3.0× |
| `sint-fib` plain | probes-on | 1016 ms | 273 ms | 3.7× |
| `float-numeric` plain | probes-off | 269 ms | 78 ms | 3.5× |
| `float-numeric` plain | probes-on | 277 ms | 75 ms | 3.7× |
| `sint-list` plain | probes-off | 151 ms | 43 ms | 3.5× |
| `sint-list` plain | probes-on | 174 ms | 42 ms | 4.1× |

Range across runs is **3.0×–4.1×**; call it ~3.5×. Between-workload differences are not resolvable — the ordering flips run to run.

### The limitation worth stating plainly

These workloads are **compute-heavy programs that are textually tiny** — the opposite shape from the editor, where programs are large and each evaluation is short. That shape is precisely why evaluation dominates statics here.

So the defensible claim is **"the evaluator is ~3.5× faster under wasm_of_ocaml"**, not "Hazel is ~3.5× faster". Establishing the latter needs a benchmark shaped like real editing — large programs, short evaluations, statics on the hot path — which this harness deliberately isn't. Worth building separately if the app-level number is what matters for the decision.
